utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Brdjanin, can you hear me in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I can hear and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down and good morning to you. Appearances for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Joanna Korner and Nicholas Koumjian assisted by Ruth -- excuse me, Denise Gustin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman, I'm with Milan Trbojevic and Marela Jevtovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What a better memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, he's not here all the time, I am. And it's Happy New Year to people from Serbia and Republika Srpska and places like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Good -- Happy New Year to all of them too. Now, I understand that there is some urgent matter you would like to rise in closed session before we bring in the witness. Is that correct? Private or --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Private, okay. So we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, good morning to you and sorry for this short delay, but we needed to discuss something before we continued with and finished with your testimony. Please repeat your solemn declaration once more. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. And, Mr. Ackerman, hopefully will finish with you in a short while. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Sivac.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think we can finish rather quickly here this morning. Just a few little brief things. In your 1994 statement to the Prosecutor, you talked at length about the April 30th, 1992, takeover of Prijedor. And one of the things you said in connection with that was: "Muslims and Croats lost their jobs immediately." That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Most of the Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: With regard to Kozarac, in your statement to the German authorities, you made this statement: "I heard from a reliable source that of all the paramilitary units involved in the operation, the gypsy Brigade under the leadership of a man known as Cigo from Omarska was said to be the worst." Do you stand by that statement?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In that 1993 statement that you made in Zagreb, you're quoted as saying this: "Apart from the persons mentioned, the paramilitary formations that arrived from Slavonia and Banja, the so-called Arkan men, Seselj men, and among others were particularly prominent in killing the civilian population." Is that a true statement?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those units were very bloodthirsty too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How do you know that they were Arkan and Seselj men?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we know. All of us know. All the inhabitants of Prijedor know that these were paramilitary units of Zeljko Arkan and Vojislav Seselj because they were characteristically dressed. And right across the street from where I lived, where a friend of mine, a single man lived, Ljubo Tumbas moved in. He was a hard core criminal from Serbia. For a long time before 1992, he was serving a prison sentence for murder. As he stayed in the building where my friend lived, across the street, he said that quite openly, that he is a member of the units of Zeljko Raznjatovic Arkan and that they had come to Prijedor to do the dirtiest jobs, inter alia. This man, this human being, or rather this inhumane being was called Ljubo Tumbas, and in Serbia in the ex-Yugoslavia, he served long-term prison sentences because he had taken part in several murders. The kind of person I am, a principled person, I like to investigate things, and I found this periodical called Ilustrovana Politika from way back. And I found an article entitled "Ljubo Tumbas Accused of a Murder of a Married Couple." Their last name was Tocilovac [phoen], as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: After you left Omarska, you went to Trnopolje. Did you see any machine-guns in Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all the guards who were at their guard posts were very well armed. There was a variety of weapons, lighter machine-guns, heavier machine-guns, automatic rifles, as we call them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Were there any what we could call machine-gun nests that you saw?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. That's what we called these places.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can you just very briefly tell the Court where these were located in Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you going to sustain a question without showing the witness at least a diagram, a sketch, of the layout of Trnopolje? Because --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm hoping I don't have to go to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If he's in a position to answer your question without the need of -- without the help of a sketch, yes, please go ahead. If you need a diagram sketch of the layout of the camp, tell us and it can be dug up easily without any problems.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A diagram is not needed. Around the camp of Trnopolje, when I arrived, there were several of these machine-gun nests. This is where guards were and they were surrounded by sandbags. They were at a certain distance from the Trnopolje camp. At guard post number 1 - I have to tell you about this - a colleague of mine was on guard duty. Before 1992, he worked with me as a journalist for ten years. His name was Boro Grubic. Together with him, at guard post number 1 was another guard, Zoran Kneginic, also a colleague of mine from Prijedor. Let me mention one more thing to the honourable Trial Chamber. For us, the camp inmates who had come from Omarska and Keraterm, Trnopolje was sheer salvation. It was a five-star hotel for us, and I'll tell you why. At the guard posts around the camp of Trnopolje there were guards who were actually our acquaintances from Prijedor. After all, these were men that we knew well and they knew us well. It wasn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you satisfied with the answer, Mr. Ackerman? Do we have to go through all this or do you have a further question to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have one more question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How many of these machine-gun nests would you say there were?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to say the following: The approximate number of machine-gun nests, as far as I could see, because I could not walk around the entire camp of Trnopolje, as far as I can remember, there were three. One guard post or as we call it this machine-gun nest was at the very crossroads of the roads by Trnopolje, the road that comes from Garevci and goes towards the railway station. That was guard post number 2. Cedo Mandic often stood guard there, a retired policeman, and he was very rough on us. There were some other guards --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, my only question was how many, how many that you saw, not who stood guard there or -- how many.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three, three guard posts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Next question, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's all I have, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to go back now to this delegation that you claim to have seen in Omarska. I want to ask you about Srdjo Srdic. Was he present in this that group?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you see Srdjo Srdic in Omarska more than that one time?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I saw him only then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You told us yesterday that you first said Kupresanin was a member of the delegation because you had gotten him confused with Stojan Zupljanin. Isn't that what you said?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already said that I've confused Stojan Zupljanin with Kupresanin. Actually, I knew Stojan Zupljanin very superficially [As interpreted], very well [Realtime transcript read in error "very well"], and I confused him with Kupresanin. Vojo Kupresanin was not in Omarska at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I want to get a clarification of the translation. It was translated I knew Stojan Zupljanin superficially, very well -- okay, but I see the transcript doesn't have that any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. But you've said it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I don't think that's what the witness said but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We are going there, Mr. Koumjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You worked for SUP for quite some time, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In connection with that work, you must have known Stojan Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. On the 1st of January, 1990, I left the security service and I only devoted myself to my duties as a journalist. Stojan Zupljanin, I don't know when he came to head the police in Banja Luka. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The person who you saw at Omarska, who you said you confused with Kupresanin but really was Stojan Zupljanin, was that person wearing a police uniform?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You know that Zupljanin would have been wearing a police uniform, don't you?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know if he ever wore a police uniform but I know that at that time he wore civilian clothes, and that's what led to the confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Didn't the police always wear police uniforms?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Policemen, but their high officials, very seldom.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you have any reason to try to protect Vojo Kupresanin?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, none whatsoever. I don't wish to protect that person at all, nor do I have any reason to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You told us yesterday that you met Mr. Brdjanin for the first time in 1988. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how this was translated, but I'll tell you something. As I worked as a journalist during --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir my question is: Did you first meet him in 1988 or not. That's my only question.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps even earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Were you in Croatia during any part of 1988?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1988? No, no, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you didn't see Mr. Brdjanin in Croatia in 1988?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I never said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You claim to have met him in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not in Banja Luka that I saw him. As far as I can remember, my first contact with him was in Celinac where this accused person of yours was head of a construction company. It was before 1998 -- 1988, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. When you claim to have seen Mr. Brdjanin in Omarska, did you have a chance to observe him well?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you have in your mind as you sit there, in your mind's eye, right now, a mental picture of that scene where you saw Mr. Brdjanin in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, sir, this kind of face that Brdjanin has is one that a person memorises, remembers for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My question was, do you have a mental picture in your mind as you sit here today of that scene where you saw Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, I do. I do have that picture, very well so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In that picture, what is he wearing?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember now what he was wearing. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You put the question yesterday, Mr. Ackerman, and he answered it. He said that he was wearing civilian clothes and that's it. He couldn't remember anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I was trying to help him with his memory, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You think that today maybe you can the witness to --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yesterday, he remembers more? Come on. Next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When the foreign journalists came to Omarska, you told us yesterday that certain people were hidden from those journalists. Who were the people who were hidden from the journalists?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Esad Sadikovic was hidden from the journalists.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Who else? Anybody?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, only Dr. Esad Sadikovic, as far as I know on the basis of the place where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So it was very well known throughout the Omarska camp that foreign journalists had been there?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We didn't know at that time, on that day. We didn't know why we were detained in those premises almost the entire day or during the entire morning, and we were not supposed to show any sign of life, only much later sir that I realise what this was all about. You have a videotape which was used in previous trials, Simo Drljaca, Zeljko Meakic, and these gentlemen were taking the journalists around and explaining things to them, saying that the conditions in the Omarska camp were very humane, and that due to the security and safety of the journalists --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... First question I asked you about this was who: Were the people that were hidden from the journalists? And you said only one person was, Sadikovic. Now you're saying that you were and another large group of people were. Several of you didn't see them. What I want to know is: Who are the people that did not see the journalists? Can you describe them in any way?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I don't know. You're trying to confuse me totally and I am very clear. Dr. Eso Sadikovic was taken into a separate room where he was hidden, whereas all the other inmates were also locked up in the rooms where they were staying except for one group of inmates who were in the hangar and they were supposed to run by the journalists and go to this other infamous place. All of us were hidden. We were all hidden in the premises of the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, I suspect that very shortly after that visit, everybody in the camp knew that foreign journalists had been there, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, approximately that's what we heard, that foreign journalists were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yesterday, you said that after the visit of the foreign journalists, the guards changed their attitude and those of you who didn't see the foreign journalists couldn't understand why they were acting differently. That's what you said, right?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I said that none of us then saw any foreign journalists. We just noticed that the guards completely changed their attitude towards us for a day or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to ask you now about your meeting with Krkan, that meeting in which you say he told you that everyone at Omarska was intended for liquidation. You recall that conversation?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When did it take place?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sometime in mid-July.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you left the camp early August, right?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. That's it, the 6th or 7th of August, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, if it's true that everyone in Omarska was intended for liquidation, why is it they weren't all killed? The guards had plenty of guns, there were plenty of people around there who could have killed you all. Why didn't that happen?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. That question should be put to the persons who are accused here and those who will come here in the future, like Zeljko Meakic and the other persons who were in charge of the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, isn't it the case that you're just making up that statement of Krkan that you were all intended for liquidation? Isn't that the truth?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is nothing but the truth. Krkan and I were together for so long that he could not but tell me the truth so that I would know what situation I was in and so that I could somehow try to get out of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You were in the same room at Omarska with Dr. Sadikovic, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... You told us yesterday that he would occasionally be called out to treat someone, even guards, because the guards would occasionally hurt each other?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And is it the case that each time he was called out, that everybody in the room would thank him for all he had done?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The last time he was called out, you told us yesterday that you thought again they were taking him out to help somebody, to treat somebody. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But you also said that you all thanked him for all he had done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Wait, wait, wait. He explained it yesterday. He said that he was also told to pick up all his belongings and take them with him and that sent a message to all the other inmates that something different was going to happen that day. And that's why they thanked him and saluted him and whatever. He gave that explanation yesterday, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So that's different?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's the way the Presiding Judge described it, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Then why did you tell us that you thought they were taking him again to help somebody? Why did you say that if you saw different?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't answer the question. Because he gave you two answers yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I won't answer it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He said yesterday that his impression that first they thought this was normal routine, but suddenly they discovered it wasn't because he was asked to pick up his belongings. So let's move to the next question, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please. I'm sorry, but, Mr. Ackerman, you are becoming increasingly unfair I'm sorry I really have to tell you that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, please don't address Mr. Ackerman like that. You address the Chamber, ask the three judges up here and not Mr. Ackerman directly, as you did. Mr. Ackerman please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You described yesterday seeing Mr. Brdjanin on television with Srdjo Srdic, and what you told us yesterday was that you remember that he congratulated the Prijedor Crisis Staff for a job well done, that they had cleansed very well. And that he had said with regard to Muslims, their pants will shake with fear. Now, in every statement you have ever given which are numerous and in every testimony you have ever given, which are numerous, you have never said this before yesterday, have you?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. On several occasions, I gave very long statements and this was a summary of the most important events that took place. If I were to describe all the details I remember concerning what happened in 1992, I think that it would be a book or rather it would consist of several volumes, and that I would talk to the investigators much, much longer, and they asked me to focus only on the most important details.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. And one of the things they asked to you focus on was your knowledge of Mr. Brdjanin, and you never told them what you said here yesterday, did you?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, because nobody asked me about Mr. Brdjanin. I mean that. How long I knew him --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Nobody asked you about Mr. Brdjanin? Do you want to see the -- do you want to see the statements, the telephone conversations, where you were specifically asked: What do you know about Mr. Brdjanin? What can you tell us about Mr. Brdjanin? Would you like to see those?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment, I said what I knew and what was in my mind. But no one insisted on any such details.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me ask you finally, sir, have you ever been diagnosed with or treated for any kind of a mental illness or condition?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Once, during recreation, I fell and broke my leg. I had a double fracture as a matter of fact, and this was the only time in my life that I had any kind of treatment. So the answer is no, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think maybe the question was misinterpreted or something. I asked you about a mental illness or condition, not physical.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Ackerman. What do you think, that I'm a mental patient?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have no idea. I just asked you the question. Thank you very much. I'm finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Is there re-examination, Mr. Koumjian?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Mr. Sivac, that brings us to an end. There are no further questions. On behalf of the Tribunal, I would like to thank you for having accepted to come over and once more give evidence in a trial here in The Hague. The usher will now escort you out of this courtroom and you will be assisted, given all the assistance you require to enable you to return home. I thank you once more and have a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could be excused at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac probably wants to speak to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Incidentally, Mr. Koumjian, before you leave, before Mr. Sivac started giving evidence yesterday, you mentioned at one point some video which you said you weren't quite sure whether you were going to tender it in evidence or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to tender all of the exhibits that were mentioned in Mr. Sivac's testimony and the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That was the second points I was going to come to, to give them the proper number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: With the help of Ruth -- I mean Ms. Gustin I have the following list: In the Stakic case, S238 which was the article about the visit of the delegation to Prijedor and the collection centres, as it states in the article, may that be marked P1547/S238? And it's also S242-4. The reason that in order to show the date we have both the -- we have a reduced picture of the whole page so that the date appears. Another article on another page, visits -- Visit Krajina Representatives in Prijedor, may that be marked P1547/S239[S242-1]. And then we had a photograph, the one that was shown yesterday during Mr. Sivac's testimony of the Omarska camp that he had drawn where the prisoners stood during the delegation marked his own location, may that be P1547/S15-2[i]? The video that was played and is referred to in his transcript is, I believe, only about two minutes long and it's an interview with Dr. Stakic concerning the attack on Kozarac and he refers to what the military called the cleansing or "ciscenje" of Kozarac. May that be marked P1547/S240-1? Let me repeat that, 1547/S240-1. There is a large map that's previously been marked. It was S14 in the Stakic trial and in this trial, just for the record, it's P1127. And then we would also be moving in a decision of the executive board of Prijedor regarding destruction of a large number of buildings and residences that was referred to in the transcript. May that be marked P1547/S243?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there any objection on the part of the Defence to the admission of any of these documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. So they are so being admitted and -- thank you. I think if you have got no further business here, Mr. Koumjian, you are relieved and you can go back to the rest of your work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Now, administrative matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, a large number arise out of Your Honour's rulings in respect of the Rule 92 matters. I don't know that I've got all the rulings with me but can I deal with them in order but -- first of all, Rule 92 bis witness 7.173, Mr. Ackerman agreed it subject to the -- being given the name of the doctor. We are -- we obtained that name and we are prepared to give it to him. So unless there is any other aspect, perhaps that -- Mr. Ackerman can confirm that he's happy for that witness to be accepted under Rule 92.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine, Your Honour. The condition has been satisfied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this one is settled.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Your Honour, Witness 7.35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I wanted to address that myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Your Honour, you ruled that as Mr. Ackerman required him for cross-examination, he had to come. Your Honour, I intend to go back -- well, I'm just going to remind Your Honour that the original ruling that Your Honours made said that reasons had to be given, not just the demand to cross-examine. Can I put it this way? It may be that we've dealt with it. I have addressed the matter with Mr. Ackerman. We are prepared to redact the parts that he requested, and again I would just like confirmation that in those circumstances, he would agree that that witness can be dealt with under Rule 92.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that was the points I was going to raise myself actually. Mr. Ackerman? Granted that the Prosecution will redact the transcripts as requested, would you still require the witness for cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour I'm having what we euphemistically call at times a senior moment. I don't remember who 7.35 is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You had, and I'm quoting directly from you in quotes, "No objection to the admission of the transcript if the redactions requested are agreed."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand that. I just need to have somebody tell me the name.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He's BT-42.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That doesn't help either.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. He's the witness who testified at length in Stakic and --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay, I know who it is now. Yes, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you will be redacting as requested?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We will be redacting as requested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the witness will not be required for cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Next, Witness 7.208. Again, Your Honour ruled that she had to be called for cross-examination. I regret to tell Your Honours she declines to attend for cross-examination. The result is that we are going to replace her evidence with another witness, 7.110, to call live.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So 7.208, there is no transcript, in other words she will not be with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: She won't attend for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And instead you will be calling live 7.110?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think he can help. It's his computer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just to make note of it. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, I thought -- Ms. Gustin was just reminding me something about it. Then, can I come next to one of the Novi witnesses? The point was made rightly by Mr. Ackerman 7.147, that we had not got a 92 bis, and that's correct. We omitted or rather we didn't notice when we put it in because it was a change there, that he hadn't been seen or the statement hadn't been read back to him. Now the problem that arises is this and we seek Your Honour's guidance. The registry, understandably, are most reluctant to send officers out just to do one 92 bis statement because of the expense. There are two alternatives, and it's really for Mr. Ackerman to agree. We can see if the witness can be taken before a local judge by an investigator, have the statement read back to him, have him attest to the truth of its contents. Whether the procedures comply with the law of the particular country, I don't know, and it would -- it would take sometime to find out. Or alternatively, one of the ways of doing it is that it's accepted without the rule -- by an investigator making a declaration to the fact that the statement has been translated back to him, and he agrees it. Now, I am in the hands of the Court, otherwise we will have to put in a formal request for the registry to send a presiding officer out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What do you have to say about that, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the rule specifically contemplates that these attestations for Rule 92 bis purposes may be made by local officials under the law of the place where the declaration is made. I've always wondered why the registry spends money to send people out to do this because it makes no sense. It can be done locally. So I'm perfectly willing to have it done locally by whatever the law, whatever the country is requires. In the U.S., it would be a ten-minute process with a notary public. I don't know what it would be in other places. But I think it's silly to have the registry sending people out to perform these tasks in the first place, but I would not be content with having some investigator certify it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I take the point, and Mr. Ackerman is right. The same would be in England, you just go before a lawyer and get it sworn. Regrettably, it isn't -- in the particular country, I know it's not as simple as that. But in the event -- if we do that, can I take it that subject to that, Mr. Ackerman will accept it? Because I'm not going to waste time going through this procedure if Mr. Ackerman at the end of the day says, no, he won't accept it anyhow and we have to call the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The possibility is envisaged by the regulations by the rules, and it's an alternative --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no, Your Honour. I'm saying that but in this particular country it isn't as simple as that. I know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I do, though. For obvious reasons, I'm not disclosing the country. Therefore all I'm saying is we will undertake that procedure provided that that's all that Mr. Ackerman's complaint is. If at the end of that he still says, I want the witness, then I will simply - if I decide to call the witness - have the witness here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Can we go along with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's -- it should be implicit in number 4 of my response that that's my position, that it's the lack of the 92 bis statement that I'm concerned about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. The -- well the obvious -- the next question is really in relation to tomorrow's witness. Mr. Ackerman said that unless he had a chance to read the war diary, he was going to object to the witness being called. But can I take it that that's gone now because we have an extra day, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Tomorrow's witness will take how long?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I would think he will take two days in chief, simply because he's going to go through videos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you think we will finish with him this week?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. I see Mr. Ackerman shaking his head.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's unlikely, Your Honour. I think I would have at least two days of cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But if that's the case, please do tell him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He knows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He's aware of that, Your Honour. The only thing that I will put back is Mr. Mayhew, who was due to attend on Friday, but I'll ask him if he can attend on Monday instead. Your Honour, this is really, as it were, a forewarning. The Stakic Defence case, as Your Honour knows, has started. And in the course of it, they called a witness who was a secretary to the Omarska camp or working in the Omarska camp. In the course of her evidence, she gave relevant evidence relating to this trial, direct evidence, and so we will be applying to call her in this case. It relates obviously to Prijedor. In addition to that, the likelihood is, and I'm just having -- we are having another check -- but another Defence witness who testified, who doesn't give direct evidence in respect of the defendant but it is relevant evidence to this case we will be seeking to put the transcript in under Rule 92, but that hasn't happened. I'm just giving prior notice of that. Now, Your Honour, in respect of a potential expert witness, can I ask to go into private session on this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session, please, as well I had the intention of raising an issue here, but I suppose you will be doing that yourself because it's quite obvious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is another matter which I would like to signal to you, that is the motion that you filed sometime back, Ms. Korner, asking -- requesting judicial notice be taken of certain matters. As a response, the Defence had suggested introducing statements via the 92 bis procedure, instead of us taking judicial notice of the facts. You had at -- if my memory does not fail me, you had indicated that -- in court during particular sitting that you had not taken the Rule 92 bis route because the witness -- witnesses would not be available for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's absolutely right. Your Honour. We didn't feel -- we've always taken the view that we can't Rule 92 bis when we know in advance the witnesses won't attend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. Now, the situation could change radically if the Defence addresses this question in particular, and indicates whether they would be asking for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour that's absolutely right. May I say this? I suppose in one sense that of course would be the pragmatic answer, and I'm not going to say -- but this rule has been sitting there forever. So far, nobody has made a ruling under Rule 94 to say that there will be adjudicated facts. It does seem to us that this is a classic case for somebody finally to rule because what possible interest can it be to the defendant or to the accused that when he's not directly named, when calling these witnesses to give that evidence again, were it possible, would elicit no doubt the same evidence again that there were these killings. And so we were anxious to have a ruling and for somebody finally to say, "Here is the classic case of an application of Rule 94 and why it should be allowed." Because otherwise we may as well scrap this rule because this is the ideal case, we think. However, Your Honour, that is my own personal plea. It's not even my personal plea. It's somebody else's on my team's personal plea. They wants a ruling. But I agree that if Mr. Ackerman agrees that the witnesses would not have to attend, then it can be dealt with by way of Rule 92.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that rule that she refers to, that judicial notice rule, I from the very beginning thought it should have been scrapped because it among other things doesn't describe a situation of judicial notice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's still there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In any event, my position is that you have got two available to you at least two ways to look at the evidence about this matter. One is some other court's conclusion that may not have been all that interested in what went on in that village and the actual transcripts of the testimony. It seems to me the best evidence is by far the actual transcripts of the testimony. I have no intention of asking any of these people be called for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. -- Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. In that case, Your Honour, can we just make the application, without having to go through the formal thing can we make the application that those transcripts are admitted under Rule 92?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there was something else occurred to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, there is something else. Let's go into private session for a while. Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was saying I thought there was something else but I can't remember what it is so I'm sure -- but I think we've dealt with the major issues that need to be dealt with so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's fine. I think so too. Would you like to raise any further matters, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We've touched on virtually everything I had in mind this morning with the exception of one and that is the calendar for the first three months of this year. What I have shows absolutely no breaks at all for three months, and I'm sure that's not correct. And I'm just wondering when we are going to get a calendar that shows breaks during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suggest you sit down together, you, Mr. Ackerman, and you, Ms. Korner, and come with some suggestions and then we will consider what the options will be. But it is very important at this point in time that we recover as much lost territory as much as possible. I had planned to finish the case for the Prosecution by April at the latest, but as I see it, that is not going to be possible and it will be unfortunate, because --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me say something about that, Your Honour, that I think is important. There are two really important things with regard to what we call breaks. We probably should call them preparations periods, because that's what they are really are. Any time I can get a week or so where I don't have to be in court, I can accomplish a great deal in terms of preparation which makes it possible for the case to go on at the pace that it's going. So if anybody has the impression that what those breaks are are times when we go skiing or lie in the sun or things of that nature, they are incredibly wrong. They are times when intense preparation work is being done and that's true for the Prosecutor as well as the Defence and I know that to be the case. The other part of that has to do with the conditions, the situation, under which Mr. Brdjanin must live. The only way that he gets to see his family is when we have those breaks. Otherwise, he cannot see his family and it becomes a horrible situation to deprive him of the ability to meet with and talk with his wife and children for extended periods of time. And it's important for his mental health, for his physical well being even, that he be able to do that. And so anybody who thinks that what we are doing is just fooling around for no good reason has got it wrong. I think we are moving this case as rapidly as we possibly can, considering the nature of it and the immense amount of material involved, and I am on the same page as you are, Your Honour, with wanting to move forward as rapidly as we can but not unreasonably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, I suggest you sit down and discuss this amongst yourselves first.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is no I hope. Your Honour, I took the view that for once there was a sensible, straightforward sitting through with no breaks, and I took the view that Your Honours must have arranged for that because of the constant breaks. Your Honour, if one looks at the Stakic case, the time that has been sat and all the rest of it and I'm sure that Dr. Stakic has the same problems as Mr. Brdjanin and that his counsel have the same problem, indeed Mr. Ostojic comes from the States, but it has been sitting without a break and indeed full days in many cases. Your Honour, I am of course in the Trial Chamber's hands but our view is that to finish this case realistically after 18 months of trial in May it is only possible if we sit as the Court schedule shows. I don't know the arrangements in the DU, but I cannot believe it is necessary to have breaks for an accused to be able to see his family because if that was right, Dr. Stakic would never have seen his family in the nine months that that trial has been running. Your Honour, with respect to Mr. Ackerman, of course it's right we use periods off for preparation but the whole points of having, as I said over and over again, two counsel, is that one counsel prepares for one witness, the other counsel praeps prepares for another witness, and whoever does the motions does that. So, Your Honour, of course it's a matter for Your Honours and I'm not going to argue if Your Honours have -- but I'm not prepared to agree it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will deal with it later on. In the meantime, I still suggest that you sit down and discuss it amongst yourselves and maybe there will be tit-for-tat approach between you. Anyway, discuss it amongst yourselves before you come back to us, Mr. Ackerman, and then we will decide. Anything else? So tomorrow, we'll have the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, and can I say that I'm grateful to Your Honours, as I say had it not been for the weather conditions last week, we would have been able to start straight away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, we are fully appreciative of the efforts that you have put in and that this was beyond your control. So don't worry about it. So the trial stands adjourned until tomorrow morning at 9.00 in this same courtroom. I thank you all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 10.39 a.m., to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 15th day of January, 2003, at 9.00 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25
